clinicalScope: Acute and chronic viral hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E) in adults and children presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Viral Hepatitis
subject: Medicine
summary: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver, often caused by viruses that spread through food, water, blood or sex. In East Africa the most common are hepatitis A, B, C and E, each with distinct ways of spreading, clinical courses and long‑term risks.

sections.p: Viral hepatitis is liver inflammation caused by hepatotropic viruses. In sub‑Saharan Africa, hepatitis B prevalence is 6‑10 % and hepatitis C 1‑3 %; hepatitis A and E cause frequent outbreaks linked to poor sanitation.
b: HBV: DNA virus, transmitted perinatally, sexually, or via unsafe injections.
HCV: RNA virus, mainly blood‑borne (unsafe transfusion, scarification).
HAV/E: RNA viruses, fecal‑oral route; HAV mainly childhood, E linked to pregnant women.
Co‑infection with HIV or malaria worsens outcomes.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the hierarchy of risk mirrors exposure routes and local practices.
b: Unsafe injection practices (traditional scarification, unsterile needles).
Perinatal transmission of HBV (high HBeAg prevalence in mothers).
Contaminated water/food (HAV, HEV outbreaks after floods).
Blood transfusion without screening (HBV, HCV).
Co‑existing HIV infection (higher chronicity, faster fibrosis).

sections.p: Viruses enter hepatocytes, trigger innate immunity, and may persist if immune clearance fails, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.
b: HBV integrates into host DNA, producing HBsAg that dampens immune response.
HCV replicates in the cytoplasm, causing continuous low‑grade inflammation.
HAV/HEV cause a self‑limited cytopathic injury with robust immune clearance.
Cytokine‑mediated cholestasis produces jaundice; loss of synthetic function causes coagulopathy.

sections.p: The clinical picture varies with virus, age and immune status.
b: Incubation: 2‑6 weeks (HAV/E), 4‑12 weeks (HBV), 6‑7 weeks (HCV).
Prodrome: malaise, anorexia, low‑grade fever, RUQ discomfort.
Icteric phase: scleral jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus.
Acute fulminant hepatitis: encephalopathy, asterixis, INR > 1.5.
Chronic HBV/HCV: often asymptomatic; may present with fatigue, hepatomegaly, or decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, variceal bleed).

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical uncover exposure routes and severity.
b: Ask about recent travel, water source, food hygiene, sexual partners, tattoos, scarification, transfusions, and maternal HBV status.
Screen for HIV, TB, malaria co‑infection.
Examine for scleral icterus, spider nevi, palmar erythema, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites (shifting dullness), and asterixis.
Check for stigmata of chronic liver disease (caput medusae, gynecomastia).

sections.p: Many conditions mimic viral hepatitis; prioritize based on epidemiology and labs.
b: Drug‑induced liver injury (e.g., rifampicin, isoniazid).
Acute malaria‑related hemolysis with hyperbilirubinemia.
Leptospirosis (Weil disease).
Autoimmune hepatitis (rare but possible).
Biliary obstruction (gallstones, cholangitis).

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Interpretation follows a stepwise algorithm; when a test is unavailable, use clinical surrogates.

t.b: Is there hepatocellular injury? ALT > 5 × ULN suggests acute viral or drug injury.
Is cholestasis present? Direct bilirubin > 2 mg/dL indicates intra‑hepatic cholestasis.
Acute vs chronic HBV? HBsAg + anti‑HBc IgM = acute; HBsAg + anti‑HBc IgG = chronic.
Identify fecal‑oral hepatitis; positive IgM = recent infection.
Confirm chronic HCV; antibody + RNA = active infection.
Assess synthetic function; INR > 1.5 indicates impaired liver synthesis.
Detect liver size, fibrosis signs, ascites, portal vein diameter.

sections.p: Acute hepatitis is staged by clinical course; chronic HBV/HCV use WHO fibrosis scores and Child‑Pugh classification for cirrhosis.
b: Acute severe: INR > 1.5, encephalopathy, bilirubin > 10 mg/dL.
Chronic HBV: HBeAg status, HBV DNA level, ALT > 2 × ULN, FibroScan > 7 kPa.
Child‑Pugh A‑C: based on bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy.
WHO fibrosis stage: F0‑F4 based on APRI (AST/ALT ratio) when imaging unavailable.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities common in East Africa modify presentation and management.
b: HIV co‑infection accelerates HBV/HCV progression; antiretroviral drugs may be hepatotoxic.
Malaria or TB treatment (rifampicin) can cause drug‑induced hepatitis.
Traditional herbal remedies (e.g., kava, cassava) add hepatotoxic risk.
Pregnancy increases risk of fulminant HEV and vertical HBV transmission.

sections.p: Treat the underlying virus, support liver function, and prevent complications; avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
b: Acute HAV/HEV: supportive care (hydration, anti‑emetics, vitamin K if INR > 1.5).
Acute HBV: consider nucleos(t)ide analogues (e.g., tenofovir) if severe (INR > 1.5, encephalopathy).
Chronic HBV: first‑line tenofovir or entecavir; monitor HBV DNA every 6 months.
Chronic HCV: pan‑genotypic direct‑acting antivirals (e.g., sofosbuvir/velpatasvir) where available; otherwise refer.
Avoid NSAIDs, isoniazid, rifampicin unless benefits outweigh risk.
Treat co‑infections (antiretroviral therapy, anti‑TB drugs with liver‑sparing regimens).
Vaccinate susceptible contacts (HBV vaccine, HAV vaccine if outbreak).
Fulminant hepatic failure: encephalopathy, INR > 2, asterixis – requires transfer to ICU/ transplant centre.
Decompensated cirrhosis: ascites, variceal bleed, hepatic encephalopathy.
Hepatocellular carcinoma: AFP > 400 ng/mL or focal lesion on ultrasound.
Coagulopathy: spontaneous bruising, prolonged PT.

sections.p: Tailor care for children, pregnant women and HIV‑positive patients.
b: Infants born to HBsAg‑positive mothers: give birth‑dose HBV vaccine + HBIG within 24 h.
Pregnant women with HEV genotype 1: monitor closely; consider early delivery if fulminant.
HIV‑positive: use tenofovir‑based ART that also suppresses HBV.
Children with HAV: usually self‑limited; ensure re‑hydration.

sections.p: Long‑term outcomes depend on virus type and treatment adherence.
b: Acute HAV/HEV: full recovery in >95 % of immunocompetent adults.
Chronic HBV: 5‑year risk of cirrhosis 10‑20 % without treatment; antiviral therapy reduces risk by >50 %.
HCV: cure rates >95 % with DAAs; untreated leads to cirrhosis in 20‑30 % over 20 years.
Screen all pregnant women for HBsAg; vaccinate newborns.
Community measures: safe injection practices, clean water, hepatitis B vaccination (birth dose + 2‑dose schedule).

sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
b: Anti‑HBc IgM may be negative in early acute HBV; repeat after 1 week if suspicion high.
ALT may be normal in chronic HBV with immune tolerance phase; rely on HBV DNA and fibrosis assessment.
HEV IgM can cross‑react with other viral antibodies; confirm with PCR if available.
INR may be normal early in fulminant hepatitis; monitor trend.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of confusion or asterixis
Rapidly rising bilirubin >10 mg/dL with INR > 1.5

faq.q: Can hepatitis be transmitted through casual contact?
faq.a: No. Only blood, sexual fluids, perinatal exposure, or fecal‑oral routes spread the viruses.

faq.q: Why is hepatitis B more likely to become chronic than hepatitis A?
faq.a: HBV integrates into host DNA and evades immune clearance, while HAV is cleared quickly by the immune system.

faq.q: Is a normal ALT enough to rule out serious liver disease?
faq.a: No. In early chronic HBV or in immune‑tolerant phase ALT can be normal despite ongoing damage.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man with jaundice, ALT 1200 U/L, INR 1.6 – what is the next immediate management step? — Assess for fulminant failure; start tenofovir if HBV suspected and arrange ICU transfer.
How does the presence of HBeAg alter the prognosis of chronic HBV? — Indicates high viral replication and greater risk of cirrhosis; warrants antiviral therapy.
Which serologic pattern distinguishes acute HBV from chronic infection? — HBsAg + anti‑HBc IgM (acute) vs HBsAg + anti‑HBc IgG (chronic).
A pregnant woman in her third trimester tests HBsAg‑positive, HBeAg‑negative. What prophylaxis does her newborn need? — Birth‑dose HBV vaccine plus HBIG within 24 h, then complete vaccine series.
Why is rifampicin contraindicated in a patient with active hepatitis C? — Rifampicin is hepatotoxic and can precipitate acute liver injury in already compromised livers.
Explain why APRI can be used to stage fibrosis when FibroScan is unavailable. — APRI uses AST/ALT ratio and platelet count; validated thresholds correlate with fibrosis stages.
What clinical signs differentiate cholestatic from hepatocellular jaundice? — Cholestatic: pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, elevated ALP; hepatocellular: predominant ALT/AST rise, less pruritus.

In a patient with HIV on tenofovir‑based ART who develops acute hepatitis, what is the most likely cause? — Possible HBV flare due to immune reconstitution or drug‑induced injury; evaluate HBV status.
How does hepatitis E infection differ in pregnant women compared with the general adult population? — Higher mortality, risk of fulminant liver failure, especially in third trimester.
What are the red‑flag laboratory thresholds indicating need for urgent referral in acute hepatitis? — Bilirubin >10 mg/dL, INR >1.5, ALT >2000 U/L, encephalopathy grade ≥ II.
